data.title: Howard Lutnick agrees to testify as bipartisan pressure grows over Nvidia scandal
data.description: Facing bipartisan pressure, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed Thursday to testify before Congress over national security concerns regarding the expanding Nvidia scandal. The announcement comes after Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., chair of the Senate Banking Committee, sent letters Thursday to Lutnick and Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO earlier in the day after reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News. In the letters, Scott asked that Huang and Lutnick voluntarily appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. Scott requested that Lutnick testify “for a public hearing regarding recent public reports about Nvidia and the Department of Commerce’s role that raises national security concerns.” “Given the Department of Commerce’s central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations, your testimony before the Committee will be essential in our oversight of these efforts,” Scott wrote. Representatives for Huang did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Scott’s letter. Earlier Thursday, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told reporters that Lutnick should appear voluntarily, though if he doesn’t, “He may need to be subpoenaed.” Blumenthal said one thing he wants to know is, “Were export controls relaxed?” Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., said in an interview with Fox News that he’d like Lutnick to testify before Congress “ASAP,” noting concerns about chips being exported that should not have. “We have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year that would allow some of these issues to continue, to chips being exported, it appears, to defy President Trump’s orders for those exports to be stopped,” Banks said. Huang’s extramarital activity has added to concerns that Nvidia chips may have been smuggled or illegally accessed by AI companies in China. Nvidia has said that it complies with U.S. laws on exports. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told reporters on Capitol Hill Thursday that Lutnick “certainly should” testify before Congress. “I think he should be given the opportunity and the strong encouragement to do it without a subpoena,” Cramer said. “If a subpoena becomes necessary, that would be too bad. But yes, he absolutely should.” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement that Lutnick needs to “explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military.” The White House has defended Lutnick, writing in a statement that the president “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” Huang has previously praised Lutnick’s role in uplifting the U.S. efforts to lead in AI. “Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration — he’s on top of the technology and learning the industry quickly,” Huang said while appearing at a Nvidia panel alongside Lutnick in September 2025. Reps. Gregory Meeks of New York, Gabe Amo of Rhode Island and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California — top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee — signed a letter Monday demanding answers from Lutnick over the Trump administration’s “approval of advanced AI chip exports,” noting “concerning links to China” and “alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties” to Huang. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., said Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief before lawmakers. In a new letter to Huang on Thursday, Mast asked that he appear before the committee on Dec. 1 for a “closed-door, transcribed interview,” adding that a subpoena would be issued if Huang did not confirm the interview by Friday evening. Some members of Congress said they want answers from Lutnick much sooner than next month, when the Senate Banking Committee has scheduled its hearings. “Come here before Thanksgiving. Give us the facts,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said Thursday. Tillis, who is leaving Congress in January, said it would be wise for Lutnick to testify to Congress now, before Democrats take control of both chambers next year, adding the secretary “should recognize right now he’s got a lot of Republicans that are pulling for him.” “I’m not one of them, but he does,” Tillis said. “So it would seem to me that he would do himself a favor by getting in a room with Republicans, whether it’s a committee hearing or not, and lay out the facts so that he’s got a group of people that are generally going to take at face value what he says.”

data.title: Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia’s new interim CEO?
data.description: For 13 years, Colette Kress helped manage the company’s transformation from a graphics-chip maker into the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Now, she’s being asked to lead it through one of the most turbulent moments in its history. Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO Thursday following the abrupt resignation of Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company and led it for 33 years. Huang’s departure comes amid revelations of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and one of his own reports. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead,” Kress said in a press release. “Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” “I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy,” Kress said in an email to staff following her appointment, acknowledging the “extraordinarily difficult period” for the company. Kress joined the company in September 2013 after tenures at Cisco and Microsoft, where she also held finance positions. She has helped see Nvidia through its transition from a video game-focused processor manufacturer to an AI-chip powerhouse. “Having worked with Colette at Cisco, I know she understands what it takes to lead through major market transitions, build strong teams, and execute at scale,” said John Chambers, former Cisco executive chairman and CEO. “Nvidia is at a critical moment, not just for the company, but for the future of AI and America’s technology leadership. I really believe Colette’s ability to step in as interim CEO. She is an amazing leader.” Chambers, who himself has moved from a CFO to a CEO role in the past, said that despite the uncertainty a leadership change creates, he does not believe it will fundamentally alter the company’s trajectory. “Every company goes through near death experiences,” Chambers said. “Nvidia is no different. It will be a challenging next year, I think they will continue to be a leading force in the AI landscape.” Kress and Huang worked closely together. Huang long leaned on Kress during financial conferences and the company’s earnings calls to debrief the investing public about the latest developments with the company’s operations. The company’s release noted its planned earnings call will go ahead on Nov. 17. Kress is expected to lead it, five days after taking on the new role. As Nvidia grew its business to focus on AI, Kress has been instrumental in managing financial relationships. Under her watch, the company has invested heavily into the technology sector, including Intel, Nokia and a partnership with OpenAI. In the past, Kress has noted that the inability to sell to China would affect the industry in the long run, a stance echoing Huang’s. “If you are unable to sell products to them, it will have an impact,” she said in an interview to Israeli publication Globes. In a November 2025 earnings call, Kress told investors the company is not expecting data center compute revenue from China. “Sizable purchase orders never materialized in the quarter due to geopolitical issues and the increasingly competitive market in China,” Kress told investors, according to a transcript of the call. “While we were disappointed in the current state that prevents us from shipping more competitive Data Center compute products to China, we are committed to continued engagement with the U.S. and China governments and will continue to advocate for America’s ability to compete around the world.” Kress’ tenure at Nvidia has been lucrative. Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index named her as one of two new Nvidia executives whose net worth exceeded $1 billion last year, largely based on the company stock she holds. Nvidia shares dipped Thursday following the announcement of Huang’s resignation and Kress’ new position. The crisis comes at a pivotal moment for AI development in the U.S. as outfits like Anthropic and OpenAI rely on Nvidia’s dominant chip technology. Kress’ role will be to see the company through the crisis and again cast it as a reliable player in the global markets. That may be difficult, as both investors and lawmakers are probing Nvidia for details of the alleged spy plot. Huang has agreed to brief Congress on his relationship as well as the company’s security protocols. “Jensen Huang’s decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement Thursday. “They still owe Congress answers.”

data.title: Is Outlook down? Widespread outage hits Microsoft apps
data.description: CHICAGO — A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant’s suite of apps. As of around 1:30 p.m. ET, more than 120,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook — with many saying they couldn’t send and receive emails, or encountering delays. Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services. Microsoft said that it was investigating. In updates posted on social media, Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said it was aware of users “experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.” Microsoft later added that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load” — which it said was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” The company said it would begin ”redistributing” traffic to help balance the load. Microsoft did not immediately provide further information. Earlier in the day, the company said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

data.title: Jensen Huang agrees to brief Congress on interactions with alleged spy, lawmaker says
data.description: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to brief lawmakers on his interactions with the former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under scrutiny for potential chip smuggling, and Nvidia’s security protocols, according to Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich. Huang is “in discussions to find a date that works and in the right form,” Moolenaar said Thursday morning. Moolenaar, along with Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., and Rep. Eric Crawford, R-Ark., had requested the tech leader brief Congress in a letter sent Nov. 4. Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and Crawford Chairs the House Intelligence Committee. “I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation,” Moolenaar said. In their letter sent last week, the lawmakers expressed interest in learning more about the Nvidia leader’s interactions with Alice Huang. A person familiar with the matter told NBC News that Alice Huang is suspected of collaborating with China’s Ministry of State Security. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., issued a statement early Thursday slamming Huang for his involvement with the Megaspeed executive and potential national security violations. “NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws,” Warren said.
